patient.chief_complaint: Monthly episodes of tingling spreading from hand to face followed by headache — 3 years
patient.hpi:
A 32-year-old Hispanic woman was referred to the neurology clinic by her primary care physician for recurrent episodes of numbness and tingling that she has experienced monthly for approximately 3 years. Each episode begins with tingling in her left fingertips that slowly marches up the left arm to the left side of her face over 15-25 minutes. During this phase she may experience mild left facial heaviness. After the sensory symptoms resolve, she develops a severe right-sided throbbing headache (7-8/10) with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound that lasts 4-8 hours. She takes acetaminophen 1000 mg which provides only moderate relief. She has tried sumatriptan once (borrowed from a friend), which was very effective.

She has approximately 10-12 episodes per year, consistently occurring in the days before her menstrual period. She recalls her mother having similar episodes with 'numbness and headaches' that improved after menopause. She works as a school administrator and the episodes frequently interfere with work — she has had to leave early on multiple occasions. She is on no regular medications, has never smoked, drinks wine socially (2-3 glasses/week), and exercises regularly. She reports normal blood pressure at routine checks, no diabetes, no prior stroke or cardiac history, and no recent travel or infections.

On examination today (headache-free), the neurological examination is entirely normal with full strength, intact sensation, normal reflexes, and normal coordination.

family_history: Mother had episodic sensory symptoms with headache, improved after menopause (likely migraine with aura); no family history of stroke or coagulopathy

social_history.note: School administrator; non-smoker; 2-3 glasses wine/week; exercises 3x/week; married; no illicit drugs

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Cranial nerves II-XII intact. No ptosis. PERRLA. Full extraocular movements. Facial sensation symmetric.
neurological_exam.motor: Motor strength 5/5 all limbs. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.sensory: Sensation to light touch and pinprick normal throughout including bilateral upper and lower limbs.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTR 2+ symmetric. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Migraine with sensory (somatosensory) aura (G43.1), ICHD-3 criteria met; menstrually-related migraine pattern

differential.key_features: TIA is sudden onset, negative symptoms, brief (<60 min), no headache; spreading sensory march over 15-25 min is migraine aura; normal DWI; normal MRA
MS episodes are not followed by headache; no T2/FLAIR periventricular lesions; no McDonald criteria met; single tiny WMH is insufficient
Sensory seizures are typically brief (<1 min) and stereotyped; aura spreading over 15-25 minutes is characteristically migraine; no interictal EEG abnormality

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI with DWI to exclude TIA and MS
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal brain MRI; single 2mm subcortical WMH — insufficient for MS; normal DWI; no periventricular lesions

optimal_actions.action: Laboratory workup — CBC, inflammatory markers, ANA, antiphospholipid antibodies, TSH
optimal_actions.expected_finding: All values normal — no inflammatory, autoimmune, or coagulation abnormality

optimal_actions.action: Prescribe sumatriptan 100 mg for acute attacks (at headache onset)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sumatriptan effective from patient's trial; prescribe at headache onset; do not use during sensory aura

optimal_actions.action: Initiate preventive therapy — topiramate 25 mg → 50 mg BID, given MIDAS Grade IV
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Monthly frequency with MIDAS Grade IV; topiramate 25-50 mg BID first-line

optimal_actions.action: Peri-menstrual mini-prophylaxis with frovatriptan 2.5 mg BID for 6 days around menses
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Frovatriptan 2.5 mg BID for 6 days peri-menstrually is evidence-based mini-prophylaxis for menstrually-related migraine

critical_actions: Brain MRI to exclude structural secondary causes including MS and TIA
Recognize Jacksonian march of sensory symptoms over 15-25 minutes as migraine aura, not TIA
Prescribe triptan — confirmed effective from patient's trial
Initiate preventive therapy given monthly frequency and MIDAS Grade IV
contraindicated_actions: Do not start combined OCP — contraindicated in migraine with aura
Do not give triptan during sensory aura phase — wait for headache onset
Do not anticoagulate for TIA without confirmed TIA on imaging
key_reasoning_points: Sensory aura spreading slowly (15-25 minutes) from fingertips to face (Jacksonian march pattern) is characteristic of migraine cortical spreading depression, not TIA
TIA sensory symptoms are sudden-onset, maximal immediately, and typically resolve within minutes
Normal DWI definitively excludes acute ischemic event
Small PFO found but PFO closure is not indicated without prior cryptogenic stroke
Menstrually-related pattern supports estrogen withdrawal as trigger — frovatriptan mini-prophylaxis is evidence-based strategy

red_herrings.intended_effect: PFO in patient with hemisensory episodes might trigger TIA/stroke workup or closure discussion
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: PFO closure not indicated for migraine without prior stroke (PREMIUM, MIST trials negative); 5-year identical episodic history is migraine

red_herrings.intended_effect: Any WMH in a young person with sensory symptoms might raise MS concern
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Single 2mm WMH is insufficient for MS (2017 McDonald criteria require ≥2 lesions in at least 2 of 4 locations); non-specific finding in migraineurs

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Menstrual Migraine with Aura — Preventive Treatment

KEY FINDINGS:
1. MENSTRUAL MIGRAINE: Peak attacks 2 days before to 3 days after onset of menses; estrogen withdrawal is the trigger
2. MINI-PROPHYLAXIS: Frovatriptan 2.5 mg BID or naratriptan 1 mg BID starting 2 days before expected menses (6-day course); reduces attack frequency significantly
3. CONTINUOUS OCP: CONTRAINDICATED in migraine with aura (category 3-4 per WHO)
4. TOPIRAMATE: First-line preventive; reduces monthly attack frequency by ~50%; start 25 mg QHS, titrate to 50 mg BID over 4-6 weeks
5. PROPRANOLOL: Alternative first-line preventive 40-120 mg BID; effective; may affect exercise capacity
6. CGRP MONOCLONAL ANTIBODIES: Erenumab, fremanezumab — newer options for chronic migraine; effective for menstrual migraine

CONCLUSION: Mini-prophylaxis with frovatriptan peri-menstrually plus sumatriptan for breakthrough attacks. Consider topiramate if monthly prophylaxis needed.
output.summary: Peri-menstrual mini-prophylaxis (frovatriptan) recommended; combined OCP contraindicated; topiramate or propranolol for monthly prevention

output.report:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — SUMATRIPTAN PRESCRIPTION

Findings: Sumatriptan 100 mg is appropriate. No current medications to interact. No contraindications. Take at headache onset, not during sensory aura. Can repeat once after 2 hours.

CONCLUSION: Sumatriptan 100 mg (3 tablets per month initially) is safe and indicated.
output.summary: Sumatriptan 100 mg safe; no contraindications; take at headache onset

output.report:
MIGRAINE MONITORING AND MIDAS ASSESSMENT

MIDAS SCORE ESTIMATE (Migraine Disability Assessment Score):
  Days of school/work missed (3 months): 6 days
  Days productivity reduced at school/work: 12 days
  Days of household missed: 4 days
  Days productivity reduced at household: 8 days
  Days of leisure missed: 4 days
  MIDAS TOTAL: ~34 (Grade IV — Severe)

INDICATION FOR PREVENTIVE THERAPY:
  - MIDAS Grade IV (severe disability)
  - ≥4 headache days/month with moderate-severe disability
  - Failed adequate acute therapy alone
  - ICHD-3 criteria: Recommendation for preventive therapy

CONCLUSION: Grade IV migraine disability. Preventive therapy is strongly indicated.
output.summary: MIDAS Grade IV (severe disability; score ≥21) is a recognised threshold at which preventive migraine therapy is strongly indicated; topiramate (Level A) and propranolol (Level A) are established first-line preventive agents
